gloss_terse: willing, voluntary; done by free choice rather than compulsion or necessity
gloss_readable: This adjective describes actions undertaken by free will rather than under compulsion. In classical Greek it distinguished voluntary acts from those done under constraint or ignorance. Paul uses it in Philemon to emphasize that any favor Philemon shows should spring from genuine willingness, not obligation. The multilingual evidence (voluntary, voluntario, freiwillig) consistently highlights the element of free choice.

senses.1: Applied to actions or decisions made by free will, without external compulsion. Paul's usage in Philemon 1:14 stresses that Christian generosity should be voluntary, not coerced—a principle that extends to all relationships within the body of Christ. The term carries legal and ethical weight, distinguishing genuine willingness from reluctant compliance.

gloss_terse: to stretch out, extend; to spread forth (especially the hands)
gloss_readable: This verb means to spread out or extend, often used of stretching forth the hands. In Romans 10:21, Paul quotes Isaiah to describe God's patient gesture toward Israel: "All day long I have stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people." The image evokes both divine invitation and lament over rejection. Cross-linguistic renderings (extendí, étendre, ausbreiten) all capture this outward movement of extension.

senses.1: To spread out or extend, particularly the hands in a gesture of appeal or invitation. In Romans 10:21, citing Isaiah 65:2, the image depicts God's persistent outreach to rebellious Israel—hands stretched wide in both welcome and sorrow. This physical gesture becomes a powerful metaphor for divine patience and unrequited love.

gloss_terse: to fulfill, complete; to bring to full realization or completion
gloss_readable: This compound verb intensifies the basic sense of "filling" to mean bringing something to complete fulfillment. In Acts 13:33, it describes how God has fulfilled His promise by raising Jesus from the dead. The perfect tense emphasizes the completed state: the promise stands fulfilled. Multilingual glosses (ha-cumplido, accomplir) emphasize the accomplishment aspect, while the German preserves the Greek form, perhaps acknowledging its theological richness.

senses.1: To bring to full completion or realization, especially of divine promises or purposes. In Acts 13:33, Paul declares that God has fulfilled His promise to the fathers by raising Jesus—a complete, definitive act. The perfect tense underscores the lasting effect: what God promised stands accomplished, reshaping Israel's messianic hope.

gloss_terse: completion, fulfillment; the act of bringing something to full realization
gloss_readable: This noun denotes the completion or fulfillment of something, often in a temporal or ritual context. In Acts 21:26, it refers to the completion of days of purification—the moment when ritual requirements are fully met. Classical usage includes filling up measures or cycles, and the LXX uses it for filling up the measure of sins. Here it marks the endpoint of a ritual period, when obligations are satisfied.

senses.1: The completion or fulfillment of a period or process, especially ritual observance. In Acts 21:26, Paul enters the temple to announce the completion of the purification days, signaling when the offering would be made. The term captures both temporal completion (the days are finished) and ritual fulfillment (the requirements are met).

gloss_terse: to engage in sexual immorality, commit fornication; to practice illicit sexual behavior
gloss_readable: This intensified form of the root verb for sexual immorality appears in Jude 7, describing the egregious sexual sins of Sodom and Gomorrah. The compound suggests extreme or flagrant behavior, going beyond ordinary boundaries. Jude cites their "indulging in immorality" as a warning example of judgment. The multilingual glosses (fornicando, s'étant-prostituées, Unzucht-treibend) all convey the severity of the transgression, whether through ongoing aspect or intensified vocabulary.

senses.1: To engage in extreme or flagrant sexual immorality, often with the sense of going beyond normal boundaries. In Jude 7, the verb describes Sodom and Gomorrah's indulgence in sexual sin, which brought divine judgment. The compound form intensifies the sense of depravity, marking their behavior as a paradigmatic example of moral rebellion deserving punishment.

gloss_terse: to spit out, reject with contempt; to expel from the mouth in disgust
gloss_readable: This verb means to spit out, often as a gesture of disgust or rejection. In Galatians 4:14, Paul marvels that the Galatians did not despise or spit him out despite his physical affliction—they welcomed him instead. The phrase evokes visceral rejection, the kind of revulsion one shows toward something repulsive. Multilingual renderings vary: Spanish emphasizes rejection (rechazasteis), while French and German preserve the Greek form or use the literal "spit out," capturing the physical intensity of the metaphor.

senses.1: To spit out in disgust or contempt, expressing visceral rejection. In Galatians 4:14, Paul acknowledges that his physical condition could have provoked such revulsion, yet the Galatians received him warmly instead. The verb dramatizes the contrast between natural human aversion to affliction and the love shown by the Galatian believers, who saw past Paul's frailty.

gloss_terse: to pervert, twist, turn aside; to corrupt or distort morally or doctrinally
gloss_readable: This verb means to twist or turn inside out, and metaphorically to pervert or corrupt. In Titus 3:11, it describes someone who is "perverted"—twisted out of proper moral and doctrinal shape. The perfect tense indicates a settled state: such a person has become warped and remains so, sinning by their own condemnation. The image of turning or twisting (Classical usage includes feet turned outward) becomes a powerful picture of moral distortion.

senses.1: To be perverted or twisted out of proper moral or spiritual shape. In Titus 3:11, the perfect passive describes a factious person as thoroughly corrupted, beyond correction. The perfect tense implies a settled condition: they have become warped and remain so, actively sinning and self-condemned. The metaphor of physical distortion captures the comprehensive nature of their moral deviation.

gloss_terse: to disturb, agitate, throw into confusion; to unsettle emotionally or socially
gloss_readable: This verb means to throw into confusion or agitate, whether emotionally or socially. In Acts 16:20, the accusers claim that Paul and Silas are "disturbing our city"—stirring up trouble and upsetting the social order. The verb can describe emotional turmoil or social upheaval. The multilingual glosses (perturban, troubler) emphasize the unsettling effect, while German preserves the Greek form, perhaps acknowledging the specific legal-social dimension of the accusation.

senses.1: To disturb or agitate, causing social upheaval or emotional turmoil. In Acts 16:20, opponents accuse Paul and Silas of throwing their city into confusion, disrupting the established order with their teaching. The charge is both social (they're troublemakers) and implicitly religious (they challenge local customs). The verb captures the anxiety of authorities facing unwelcome change.

gloss_terse: earnestness, zeal, fervor; intense devotion or eager persistence
gloss_readable: This noun denotes earnestness, zeal, or fervent devotion. In Acts 26:7, Paul describes Israel's worship as pursued "earnestly" (literally "in earnestness") night and day. The term conveys intense, sustained devotion rather than casual observance. Classical usage includes ideas of gushing enthusiasm or assiduousness. Here it characterizes the twelve tribes' constant worship, highlighting the seriousness with which they serve God in hope of the promise.

senses.1: Earnest devotion or fervent zeal, marked by intensity and persistence. In Acts 26:7, Paul describes Israel's worship as characterized by this earnestness—they serve God constantly, night and day, in eager hope of the promise. The noun captures not just activity but the passionate spirit behind it, the kind of wholehearted devotion that perseveres without flagging.

gloss_terse: more earnestly, with greater intensity; in a heightened manner of fervor or effort
gloss_readable: This comparative adverb intensifies the idea of earnestness, describing action done with even greater fervor or intensity. In Luke 22:44, it describes Jesus praying "more earnestly" in Gethsemane, as His anguish deepened. The comparative form marks an escalation: His prayer became more intense, more urgent. The multilingual renderings (más intensamente, plus ardemment) all capture this heightening of fervor, the increase in emotional and spiritual intensity.

senses.1: With greater earnestness or intensity, describing an increase in fervor or effort. In Luke 22:44, as Jesus' agony intensifies in Gethsemane, His prayer becomes more earnest—the comparative adverb marks the deepening crisis. His intercession grows more urgent, more strenuous, as He faces the cup He must drink. The term underscores the human struggle of Jesus in His passion.

gloss_terse: earnest, fervent, intense; marked by sustained devotion and heartfelt commitment
gloss_readable: This adjective describes earnest, fervent, or intense devotion. In 1 Peter 4:8, it modifies love: "earnest love for one another." The term suggests love that is stretched out, sustained, unwavering—not casual or intermittent. Classical usage includes ideas of being warmly attached or assiduous. Peter urges a love that persists through difficulty, covering a multitude of sins. The multilingual glosses (ferviente, eifrig) emphasize the warmth and diligence of such love.

senses.1: Earnest, fervent, characterized by sustained intensity and heartfelt commitment. In 1 Peter 4:8, Peter calls for earnest love among believers—love that is constant, wholehearted, and persevering. The adjective suggests love that is stretched out and sustained, not easily withdrawn. Such love is practical and powerful, covering a multitude of sins through patient forbearance and genuine care.

gloss_terse: untimely birth, miscarriage; one born prematurely or abnormally
gloss_readable: This noun means an untimely or premature birth, often a miscarriage or stillborn child. In 1 Corinthians 15:8, Paul uses it metaphorically of himself: "last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me." The term can be self-deprecating, suggesting Paul's apostolic call came abnormally, outside the normal sequence. He was not among the Twelve during Jesus' earthly ministry, making his encounter with the risen Christ exceptional and, in a sense, "premature" compared to the other apostles.

senses.1: An untimely or abnormal birth, often a miscarriage or premature delivery. In 1 Corinthians 15:8, Paul applies the term to himself metaphorically, acknowledging that his apostolic commission came unexpectedly and outside the usual sequence. He was not a disciple during Jesus' ministry but encountered the risen Lord later, in a manner that felt anomalous—hence the vivid, somewhat startling self-description.

gloss_terse: to terrify, frighten, intimidate; to cause great fear or alarm
gloss_readable: This verb means to frighten or terrify, causing alarm or intimidation. In 2 Corinthians 10:9, Paul says he does not want to seem to be "terrifying" the Corinthians by his letters. His letters are strong, and he wants to be clear he's not trying to use fear as a weapon. The verb conveys causing fear or alarm, sometimes deliberately. The multilingual glosses (aterrorizar, effrayer, erschrecken) all emphasize the production of fear or fright.

senses.1: To frighten or terrify, causing fear or alarm in someone. In 2 Corinthians 10:9, Paul denies that he aims to terrify the Corinthians with his letters, despite their weighty tone. He wants to correct, not intimidate. The verb captures the potential emotional impact of his strong words—they could frighten—but he insists his intent is pastoral, not to cow them into submission through fear.

gloss_terse: to depart, withdraw, leave; to go out from a place or situation
gloss_readable: This verb means to depart or withdraw from a place. In Luke 21:21, Jesus warns those in Judea to flee to the mountains, and those in the city to "depart" when they see Jerusalem surrounded. The verb emphasizes leaving, getting out, evacuating. Classical usage includes emigrating or retiring from a place. The multilingual glosses (salgan, sortir) capture the sense of exiting or going out, underscoring the urgency of escape in Jesus' apocalyptic warning.

senses.1: To depart or withdraw from a place, often in the sense of evacuating or fleeing. In Luke 21:21, Jesus commands those in the city to depart when they see the signs of impending judgment on Jerusalem. The imperative conveys urgency: don't stay, get out. The verb fits the context of eschatological warning, where heeding the call to leave could mean the difference between life and death.

gloss_terse: olive grove, olive orchard; specifically, the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem
gloss_readable: This noun means an olive grove or orchard, and in the New Testament specifically refers to the Mount of Olives, the ridge east of Jerusalem. In Acts 1:12, the disciples return to Jerusalem from "the mount called Olivet" after Jesus' ascension. The location was significant in Jesus' ministry—He taught there, prayed in Gethsemane on its slope, and ascended from its summit. The name preserves the agricultural character of the site, a hillside planted with olive trees.

senses.1: The Mount of Olives (Olivet), the prominent ridge east of Jerusalem covered with olive groves. In Acts 1:12, it's the site of Jesus' ascension. The mount figured prominently in Jesus' final week: He wept over Jerusalem from its slope, taught His disciples there, and prayed in Gethsemane at its foot. The name evokes both the sacred geography and the agricultural landscape of ancient Judea.

gloss_terse: Elamites; inhabitants of Elam, a region east of Mesopotamia (modern southwestern Iran)
gloss_readable: This ethnic designation refers to the Elamites, people from Elam, an ancient kingdom east of Babylon in what is now southwestern Iran. In Acts 2:9, Elamites are among the Jewish pilgrims in Jerusalem at Pentecost who hear the apostles speaking in tongues. Their presence underscores the widespread Jewish diaspora and the international scope of Pentecost's miracle. Elam was a significant ancient civilization, and Jewish communities had existed there since the Babylonian exile.

senses.1: Inhabitants of Elam, an ancient region east of Mesopotamia. In Acts 2:9, Elamites are among the diverse crowd at Pentecost, representing the far-flung Jewish diaspora. Their inclusion in Luke's list highlights how Jews from the eastern frontier of the known world witnessed the Spirit's outpouring. The multilingual miracle enabled even these distant pilgrims to hear the gospel in their native tongue.

gloss_terse: to have less, lack; to receive or possess a smaller amount
gloss_readable: This verb means to have less, to lack, or to fall short in quantity. In 2 Corinthians 8:15, Paul quotes Exodus 16:18 about the manna: "Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack." The verb describes the miracle of sufficiency—those who gathered less did not find themselves lacking. The principle illustrates the equality and mutual care Paul urges in Christian giving: resources shared so that no one is left wanting.

senses.1: To have less or lack, to be deficient in amount. In 2 Corinthians 8:15, citing the manna story, Paul notes that those who gathered little "had no lack"—they were not disadvantaged. The verb highlights the divine provision that ensured sufficiency for all. Paul applies this to Christian generosity: when believers share, inequality is leveled, and no one suffers need while others have surplus.

gloss_terse: lightness, levity; fickleness or lack of seriousness in judgment or commitment
gloss_readable: This noun can mean physical lightness or, metaphorically, levity or fickleness. In 2 Corinthians 1:17, Paul defends himself against the charge of acting with "lightness"—making plans carelessly or capriciously. He asks rhetorically if he made his plans according to the flesh, showing fickleness (saying "Yes, yes" and "No, no" at the same time). The term implies lack of seriousness or reliability. Classical usage includes lightness of weight or, in a moral sense, frivolity.

senses.1: Levity or fickleness, indicating lack of seriousness or reliability in decisions. In 2 Corinthians 1:17, Paul denies acting with lightness when he changed his travel plans. He wasn't being capricious or insincere, making promises lightly without regard to following through. The noun captures the accusation he faces: that he's unreliable, prone to saying one thing and doing another—a charge he firmly refutes.

gloss_terse: least, smallest, most insignificant; comparative/superlative form denoting minimal degree or status
gloss_readable: This is the superlative form meaning "least" or "smallest," often used to indicate minimal significance or status. In Ephesians 3:8, Paul calls himself "the very least of all the saints"—a self-effacing description highlighting his humility. The comparative form here intensifies the superlative: less than the least. The term can describe size, time, number, or importance. Paul's use underscores the grace shown him: though least qualified, he received the privilege of proclaiming the gospel to the Gentiles.

senses.1: Least, smallest, most insignificant, often referring to status or worthiness. In Ephesians 3:8, Paul describes himself as less than the least of all saints—a double comparative emphasizing his profound sense of unworthiness. Despite being the least qualified, he was entrusted with the mystery of Christ for the Gentiles. The term expresses humility but also magnifies God's grace in using the insignificant.

gloss_terse: rebuke, reproof, conviction; the act of reproving or exposing wrongdoing
gloss_readable: This noun means rebuke, reproof, or conviction—the act of exposing and correcting wrongdoing. In 2 Peter 2:16, Balaam received "rebuke for his wrongdoing" when his donkey spoke. The term can mean refutation in argument or moral correction. Here it refers to the extraordinary rebuke that stopped Balaam's madness. The noun captures both the act of reproving and the conviction or exposure of sin that results.

senses.1: Rebuke or reproof, the act of exposing and correcting wrongdoing. In 2 Peter 2:16, Balaam received rebuke for his transgression when his donkey miraculously spoke, restraining his folly. The noun emphasizes the corrective function: the rebuke was meant to stop him from pursuing sin. The incident becomes a paradigm of how God intervenes to convict and restrain those who persist in wrongdoing.

gloss_terse: coming, arrival, advent; the act of coming or appearing
gloss_readable: This noun means coming or arrival, often used of significant appearances. In Acts 7:52, Stephen accuses his hearers' ancestors of persecuting the prophets who announced beforehand "the coming of the Righteous One." The term can refer to ordinary arrivals but here carries eschatological weight: the advent of the Messiah. Classical usage includes arrivals into life or significant entrances. The noun underscores the prophetic anticipation of Christ's first coming.

senses.1: Coming or arrival, especially of a significant or anticipated event. In Acts 7:52, Stephen speaks of the prophets foretelling the coming of the Righteous One—the Messiah. The noun highlights the prophetic foreannouncement of Christ's advent, which Israel's leaders rejected by killing both the prophets and the Messiah Himself. The term carries the weight of fulfilled messianic expectation.

gloss_terse: of ivory, made from ivory; describing material from elephant tusks
gloss_readable: This adjective means made of ivory, describing objects crafted from elephant tusks. In Revelation 18:12, it appears in the list of luxury goods traded in "Babylon"—expensive commodities whose loss merchants mourn. Ivory was a prized material in the ancient world, used for decorative inlays, furniture, and ornaments. The term evokes wealth and luxury, part of the portrait of Babylon's opulence and the judgment that destroys her commerce.

senses.1: Made of ivory, describing objects crafted from this valuable material. In Revelation 18:12, ivory articles appear among Babylon's luxury goods, symbolizing wealth and excess. The merchants weep over the loss of such trade when judgment falls. Ivory's inclusion underscores the city's materialism and the emptiness of riches when divine wrath comes—all the beautiful, costly things perish in an hour.

gloss_terse: Eliezer; Hebrew name meaning 'God is my help,' an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy
gloss_readable: This is the Greek transliteration of the Hebrew name Eliezer, meaning "God is my help." In Luke 3:29, Eliezer appears in the genealogy of Jesus, one of the ancestors between David and Jesus. The name itself is a confession of faith, reflecting the ancient Israelite practice of embedding theological truths in personal names. Several Old Testament figures bore this name, most famously Abraham's servant, but Luke refers to an otherwise unknown ancestor of Christ.

senses.1: Eliezer, an ancestor of Jesus listed in Luke 3:29. The name means "God is my help" in Hebrew, a theologically rich designation common in ancient Israel. Luke's inclusion of this name, along with many others unfamiliar from the Old Testament, underscores Jesus' full humanity and His rootedness in Israel's history—even the obscure generations between David and the exile matter in God's redemptive plan.

gloss_terse: Elisha; Hebrew name meaning 'God is salvation,' the prophet who succeeded Elijah
gloss_readable: This is the Greek form of Elisha, the prophet who succeeded Elijah in the ninth century BC. In Luke 4:27, Jesus mentions Elisha to illustrate that God's mercy extends beyond Israel's borders: many lepers were in Israel, but only Naaman the Syrian was cleansed. The reference stings His Nazareth audience, who become enraged at the implication. Elisha's ministry, marked by miracles of compassion, foreshadows Jesus' own inclusive mission to Gentiles as well as Jews.

senses.1: Elisha, the prophet who succeeded Elijah and ministered in Israel during the ninth century BC. In Luke 4:27, Jesus cites Elisha's healing of Naaman the Syrian to provoke His hearers: God's grace overflowed Israel's boundaries even in the Old Testament. The reference anticipates the scandal of Jesus' own ministry to outcasts and Gentiles, and the reaction shows how deeply this challenged Jewish assumptions.

gloss_terse: to ulcerate, be covered with sores; to suffer from open wounds or lesions
gloss_readable: This verb means to be covered with sores or ulcers, to suffer from open wounds. In Luke 16:20, it describes Lazarus in the parable, a beggar "covered with sores" who lay at the rich man's gate. The perfect passive participle suggests a settled, pitiable condition: he is thoroughly ulcerated, his body ravaged by untreated wounds. The detail heightens the contrast between Lazarus' suffering and the rich man's comfort, setting up the reversal in the afterlife.

senses.1: To be covered with sores or ulcers, suffering from festering wounds. In Luke 16:20, Lazarus is described as thoroughly ulcerated, lying helpless at the rich man's gate while dogs licked his sores. The verb paints a vivid picture of his misery and neglect, underscoring the callousness of the rich man who ignored this suffering at his doorstep. The reversal of their fates in eternity makes the parable's point unforgettable.

gloss_terse: Greece, Hellas; the Greek-speaking regions of the Mediterranean, particularly the Greek mainland
gloss_readable: This noun refers to Greece or Hellas, originally the name of a region in Thessaly but eventually applied to the entire Greek mainland and, broadly, to Greek-speaking lands. In Acts 20:2, Paul travels through Macedonia and comes to "Greece" (likely Achaia, the Roman province). The term evokes the classical world, the cultural and linguistic sphere Paul navigated in his missionary journeys. His time in Greece included significant ministry in Corinth and Athens.

senses.1: Greece or Hellas, referring to the Greek mainland and broader Hellenic world. In Acts 20:2, Paul's travels take him to Greece, where he spends three months—likely in Corinth. The region represents the intellectual and cultural heart of the Mediterranean, where Paul engaged both Jews and Greeks with the gospel, debating philosophers in Athens and establishing churches amid the vibrant, morally complex cities of the Roman East.

gloss_terse: Elmadam; an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy, otherwise unknown
gloss_readable: This name appears in Luke 3:28 as one of Jesus' ancestors in the genealogy tracing His lineage back to Adam. Elmadam is otherwise unknown, one of the many names Luke includes that don't appear in the Old Testament. The inclusion of such obscure figures underscores the completeness of Luke's genealogical record and the historical rootedness of Jesus' humanity. Every generation, known or unknown, is part of God's patient work bringing the Messiah into the world.

senses.1: An ancestor of Jesus listed in Luke 3:28, otherwise unknown in biblical or historical records. Luke's genealogy includes many such names, emphasizing Jesus' deep roots in Israel's past and His full participation in human history. Even the forgotten generations matter in God's redemptive plan—each link in the chain leading from Adam to Christ contributes to the story of salvation.

gloss_terse: Elymas; the Greek or Arabic name of Bar-Jesus, the magician who opposed Paul on Cyprus
gloss_readable: This name refers to the magician who opposed Paul and Barnabas on Cyprus in Acts 13:8. Also called Bar-Jesus, Elymas was a Jewish false prophet in the court of the proconsul Sergius Paulus. When he tried to turn the proconsul away from the faith, Paul struck him blind. The name "Elymas" may derive from an Arabic or Aramaic word for "magician" or "wise man," parallel to the term "magus." His opposition and judgment serve as a dramatic confrontation between the gospel and occult power.

senses.1: Elymas, also known as Bar-Jesus, a Jewish magician who opposed Paul on Cyprus. In Acts 13:8, he attempts to prevent the proconsul Sergius Paulus from believing the gospel. Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, rebukes him and strikes him blind—a sign demonstrating the superiority of God's power over magic. The incident results in the proconsul's conversion and showcases the early church's clash with pagan religious practices.

gloss_terse: to cast in, throw into; to hurl or deposit something into a place
gloss_readable: This verb means to throw in, cast into, or deposit something into a place. In Luke 12:5, Jesus warns to fear the one who, after killing, has authority "to cast into hell." The verb emphasizes the act of throwing or consigning someone to a place—here, Gehenna. Classical usage includes throwing things to animals or laying things into someone's hands. The term underscores divine authority and the finality of judgment: God can cast into hell, a fate more fearful than physical death.

senses.1: To cast or throw into a place, often with force or finality. In Luke 12:5, Jesus warns of God's authority to cast into hell after death. The verb highlights the active judgment of consigning someone to Gehenna, the place of final punishment. This power to cast into eternal perdition belongs to God alone, making Him the one truly to be feared above all human threats.

gloss_terse: to enter into, intrude, take possession of; to step into or meddle in something
gloss_readable: This verb can mean to enter into, intrude, or take possession of something. In Colossians 2:18, Paul warns against those who disqualify believers, "insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions." The phrase "entering into" (or "dwelling on") visions suggests intruding into visionary experiences or taking unwarranted possession of mystical insights. Classical usage includes entering sacred caves or taking possession of an inheritance. Paul's point: such practices are presumptuous and lead astray.

senses.1: To enter into or intrude upon, often in the sense of meddling in or claiming access to something. In Colossians 2:18, the verb describes false teachers who claim privileged visionary experiences, "entering into" things they've seen. Paul critiques this intrusive mysticism as puffed up and disconnected from Christ. The verb suggests overreaching—intruding into realms beyond one's rightful place, whether mystery rites or angelic visions.

gloss_terse: to put on board, embark; to cause someone to board a ship
gloss_readable: This verb means to put someone on board a ship, to cause to embark. In Acts 27:6, a centurion finds an Alexandrian ship sailing to Italy and "put us on board." The verb emphasizes the action of the centurion arranging passage and getting Paul and his companions onto the vessel. Classical usage includes putting troops on ships or setting dislocated joints (putting bones back in place). Here it's straightforward: facilitating embarkation for the voyage to Rome.

senses.1: To put on board a ship, to embark someone. In Acts 27:6, the centurion arranges for Paul and his companions to board an Alexandrian vessel bound for Italy. The verb captures the logistical act of transferring passengers onto a ship, a necessary step in Paul's dramatic journey to Rome. What begins as routine embarkation will become a harrowing voyage, shipwreck, and ultimately safe arrival—a journey full of providence.

gloss_terse: to vomit, spew out; to eject from the mouth in disgust or illness
gloss_readable: This verb means to vomit or spew out, whether from illness or disgust. In Revelation 3:16, the risen Christ warns the Laodicean church: "Because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth." The verb conveys visceral rejection—lukewarmness provokes a nauseating response, leading to expulsion. The image is deliberately shocking: spiritual mediocrity is so repulsive to Christ that He will vomit out those who remain in it. The threat aims to provoke repentance.

senses.1: To vomit or spew out, expressing disgust or rejection. In Revelation 3:16, Jesus warns the lukewarm Laodiceans that He will vomit them out of His mouth. The metaphor is visceral and shocking, likening their spiritual state to something nauseating, intolerable. Neither hot (zealous) nor cold (useful for refreshment), they provoke revulsion. The stark image urges urgent repentance before judgment falls.

gloss_terse: to be enraged, mad with fury; to be driven to extreme anger against someone
gloss_readable: This verb means to be enraged or mad with fury, often directed at someone. In Acts 26:11, Paul recalls his pre-conversion zeal: "I was so enraged at them that I even pursued them to foreign cities." The present participle suggests ongoing fury—he was constantly enraged, driven by fanatical anger to persecute Christians beyond Judea. The verb captures the intensity of his opposition, a madness that later becomes a testimony to the transforming power of encountering Christ.

senses.1: To be enraged or mad with fury, driven by intense anger against someone. In Acts 26:11, Paul describes his former self as being enraged against Christians, pursuing them even to foreign cities in his zeal to destroy the church. The verb conveys irrational, fanatical anger—a fury that knew no bounds. His testimony of such rage magnifies the grace that stopped him and turned him into the apostle to the Gentiles.

gloss_terse: Immanuel; Hebrew name meaning 'God with us,' a messianic title applied to Jesus
gloss_readable: This is the Greek transliteration of the Hebrew name Immanuel, meaning "God with us." In Matthew 1:23, the angel interprets the virgin birth by quoting Isaiah 7:14: the child will be called Immanuel. The name encapsulates the mystery of the incarnation—God dwelling among His people in human flesh. Though Jesus was not literally named Immanuel, the title expresses His identity and mission: in Him, God is truly present with us, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy in a way far exceeding its original context.

senses.1: Immanuel, meaning 'God with us,' a messianic title from Isaiah 7:14 applied to Jesus in Matthew 1:23. The name expresses the theological heart of the incarnation: God has come to dwell with His people. In the virgin-born child, the divine presence takes up residence in human history. The name becomes a confession of faith, recognizing Jesus as the fulfillment of Israel's deepest hope—God's personal, saving presence.

gloss_terse: Emmaus; a village near Jerusalem where Jesus appeared to two disciples after His resurrection
gloss_readable: This place name refers to a village about seven miles (sixty stadia) from Jerusalem. In Luke 24:13, two disciples are walking to Emmaus on the day of Jesus' resurrection when the risen Lord joins them, though they don't recognize Him. He expounds the Scriptures concerning Himself, and their hearts burn within them. Only when He breaks bread do they recognize Him—then He vanishes. Emmaus becomes the setting for one of the most beloved post-resurrection appearances, a story of eyes opened and faith rekindled.

senses.1: A village about seven miles from Jerusalem, the destination of two disciples on resurrection day. In Luke 24:13, they walk to Emmaus, joined by the unrecognized risen Jesus who opens the Scriptures to them. When He breaks bread, their eyes are opened and they recognize Him. Emmaus becomes a place of revelation and transformed understanding, where sorrow turns to joy and confusion gives way to faith.

gloss_terse: Hamor; Hebrew name meaning 'donkey,' the Canaanite prince from whom Abraham bought land at Shechem
gloss_readable: This is the Greek form of Hamor, the Hivite prince of Shechem who sold land to Abraham (Genesis 33:19). In Acts 7:16, Stephen mentions this land purchase in his speech, though he conflates details from Abraham's purchase at Shechem and the burial at Hebron. Hamor was the father of Shechem, who defiled Dinah, leading to the violent revenge by Jacob's sons. The name appears in the account of Israel's patriarchal history, marking the acquisition of land that would become significant in Israel's settlement.

senses.1: Hamor, the Hivite prince of Shechem who sold land to Abraham in Genesis 33:19. In Acts 7:16, Stephen references this transaction in his historical survey. The mention evokes the patriarchal period when Abraham and Jacob acquired property in the Promised Land. Though the historical details in Stephen's speech are compressed, the reference to Hamor anchors Jesus' story in Israel's long history of sojourning and settlement.

gloss_terse: to walk among, dwell among; to move about within a community, living in close fellowship
gloss_readable: This compound verb means to walk about among or dwell among people. In 2 Corinthians 6:16, Paul quotes the Old Testament promise: "I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God." The verb emphasizes God's active, personal presence among His people—not distant but moving among them in intimate fellowship. Classical usage includes walking to and fro at a gathering. Paul applies this to the church as God's temple: the Spirit dwells and walks among believers.

senses.1: To walk or dwell among, indicating active presence and fellowship within a community. In 2 Corinthians 6:16, Paul cites God's promise to walk among His people as their God. The verb conveys not static residence but dynamic presence—God moving among His people, involved in their lives. For the church, this means the Holy Spirit actively dwells in the believing community, making them God's living temple.

gloss_terse: braiding, plaiting; the act of weaving hair into ornamental styles
gloss_readable: This noun refers to braiding or plaiting, especially of hair. In 1 Peter 3:3, Peter instructs women that their adornment should not be external—"braiding the hair and wearing gold jewelry or fine clothes." He's not forbidding these things absolutely but warning against making external appearance the focus of one's identity. Classical usage includes the interweaving of roots or mathematical interlacement. Peter contrasts outward adornment with the inner beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious to God.

senses.1: The braiding or plaiting of hair into ornamental styles. In 1 Peter 3:3, Peter cautions against letting external adornment—elaborate hairstyles, gold jewelry, fine clothes—define a woman's beauty. He's not forbidding such things but urging priorities: the imperishable beauty of a gentle, humble spirit far outweighs costly grooming. The noun symbolizes the temptation to invest in outward appearance at the expense of inward godliness.

gloss_terse: to breathe, blow; to be alive, have life and breath
gloss_readable: This verb means to breathe, blow, or simply to be alive. In Acts 9:1, Saul is described as "breathing threats and murder against the disciples." The participle suggests he was exhaling hostility—his very breath was filled with menace toward Christians. Classical usage includes breathing upon something, playing a wind instrument, or simply living. Here the metaphor is vivid: Saul's life was consumed with violent opposition to the church, every breath dedicated to persecution, until Christ stopped him on the road to Damascus.

senses.1: To breathe or exhale, often metaphorically describing one's dominant attitude or disposition. In Acts 9:1, Saul is breathing threats and murder against the disciples—his whole being exudes hostility toward Christians. The image is powerful: persecution isn't an occasional act but the very air he breathes, his consuming passion. This makes his conversion all the more dramatic: the man breathing death becomes the apostle proclaiming life.

gloss_terse: commerce, trade, business; the activity of buying and selling goods, especially by sea
gloss_readable: This noun means commerce or trade, often referring to mercantile business conducted by sea. In Matthew 22:5, it appears in the parable of the wedding feast: those invited "went away, one to his farm, another to his business." The term represents the worldly preoccupations that cause people to reject the king's invitation. Classical usage emphasizes sea trade, but broadly it means any commercial enterprise. The parable warns that even legitimate business can become a distraction from responding to God's call.

senses.1: Commerce, trade, or business activity, especially mercantile enterprise. In Matthew 22:5, it represents the worldly concerns that lead people to ignore the king's invitation to the wedding feast. One goes to his farm, another to his business—both legitimate pursuits, yet they become excuses for refusing the summons. The noun symbolizes how earthly preoccupations, however respectable, can blind us to God's invitation and lead to judgment.
